name: Melbourne
tagline: Laneway coffee, the arts and Australia's finest tables.
whenBlurb: Autumn and spring are kindest, bookended by the Australian Open in January and the Spring Racing Carnival in November; the city is famous for four seasons in a day.

ourTake.lede: Melbourne hides itself on purpose, the good coffee, bars and shops are down the laneways and up the stairs, not on the main streets. Give it to walking, eating and the arts rather than a checklist, and let the neighbourhoods do the talking. The one thing worth building a trip around is a major event; the sport and festival calendar here is genuinely world-class.
ourTake.comeIf: You want laneway coffee, world-class dining and wine country an hour away.
ourTake.skipIf: You want reliable sun or a short flight.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

A landmark grand hotel of Melbourne
items.description: Australia's grand Victorian hotel, opposite Parliament since 1883, old-world grandeur and a legendary afternoon tea.

items.name: QT Melbourne
credentials: A landmark QT design hotel of the CBD
items.description: A playful, fashion-forward design hotel with one of the city's liveliest rooftop bars.

items.name: Ovolo South Yarra
credentials: A landmark Ovolo design hotel of South Yarra
items.description: A bright, art-splashed design hotel on Chapel Street, colour, fun and generous inclusions.

items.name: Federation Square
items.description: Melbourne's angular civic heart, facing Flinders Street Station across the river, a good first anchor for orienting the city, with the Ian Potter Centre and ACMI opening off the plaza. A private guide can start you here and walk you into the laneways within minutes.

items.name: Hosier Lane street art
items.description: The most famous of Melbourne's graffiti bluestone lanes, a wall-to-wall canvas that changes weekly and runs off Flinders Lane opposite Fed Square. Even a short walk-through gives the family the city's counter-culture in ten minutes; nearby Rutledge Lane extends it.

items.name: Degraves Street
items.description: A narrow cobbled lane packed with awning-shaded cafe tables, the postcard of Melbourne's coffee culture. Order a flat white standing at a hole-in-the-wall roaster and watch the city's obsession up close.

items.name: The Block Arcade & Royal Arcade
items.description: Two exquisitely preserved Victorian-era shopping arcades: the Block with its mosaic-tiled floor and the historic Hopetoun Tea Rooms, and Royal Arcade with its Gog and Magog figures. Genteel, unhurried and a lovely stop between laneways for tea and chocolate.

items.name: National Gallery of Victoria, International (NGV)
items.description: Australia's oldest and most-visited public gallery, whose St Kilda Road building holds the international collection behind a famous water-wall entrance. The blockbuster summer exhibitions and the stained-glass Great Hall ceiling are worth timed tickets; entry to the permanent collection is free.

items.name: NGV Australia, Ian Potter Centre
items.description: The Fed Square site of the NGV devoted entirely to Australian art, including the country's most significant collection of Indigenous art. A shorter, focused visit that pairs naturally with Federation Square for a multi-generation morning.

items.name: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria
items.description: Thirty-eight hectares of lakes, lawns and rare plantings sweeping down toward the river, Melbourne's green lungs and an easy, buggy-friendly wander for elders and children alike. Take the Aboriginal Heritage Walk or an Punt Road picnic; the Tan track circles it.

items.name: Shrine of Remembrance
items.description: Melbourne's grand war memorial on a rise above the Botanic Gardens, its ceremonial forecourt and city views making it one of the CBD's most dignified vantage points. Climb to the balcony for the sightline straight down Swanston Street to the city.

items.name: Queen Victoria Market
credentials: Victorian Heritage Register, listed 19th-century market
items.description: A sprawling 19th-century open-air market, delis, produce, seafood and the Winter/Summer Night Markets, and the best single place to graze the city's food cultures in one visit. A guided Ultimate Foodie tour lets the family taste widely without the crush.

items.name: Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG)
items.description: The spiritual home of Australian sport and one of the world's great stadiums, holding 100,000 for AFL and cricket. A behind-the-scenes tour of the members' rooms and the arena thrills any sports-loving traveller; a Boxing Day Test or an AFL final is a bucket-list day.

items.name: National Sports Museum
items.description: Inside the MCG, an immersive museum of Australian sport, cricket, AFL, the Olympics and the Australian Open, with interactive galleries the children will not want to leave. Combine it with the stadium tour.

items.name: Melbourne Skydeck (Eureka Tower)
items.description: The Southern Hemisphere's highest public viewing platform, on the 88th floor at 285m, with 360-degree views and 'The Edge' glass cube that slides out over the city. Best at dusk to catch daylight then the lit skyline; the recently rebranded Eureka Skydeck.

items.name: State Library Victoria
items.description: One of the world's most beautiful reading rooms, the domed octagonal La Trobe Reading Room, free to enter and quietly spectacular from the upper galleries. A serene pause from the CBD, and home to the Ned Kelly armour.

items.name: Immigration Museum
items.description: Housed in the old Customs House, it tells the story of the peoples who built Melbourne, a resonant stop for Indian families, tracing the migration threads that make the city so plural today.

items.name: Royal Exhibition Building & Carlton Gardens
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Royal Exhibition Building and Carlton Gardens
items.description: Australia's first UNESCO-listed building, a soaring 1880 exhibition palace set in formal Victorian gardens beside Melbourne Museum. Time a dome-promenade tour; the gardens are a lovely picnic setting for elders and children.

items.name: Melbourne Museum
items.description: A modern natural-history and cultural museum beside the Exhibition Building, with the Bunjilaka Aboriginal Cultural Centre, a living rainforest gallery and the beloved racehorse Phar Lap. Genuinely absorbing across three generations, and there is an IMAX alongside.

items.name: Fitzroy, Brunswick Street & Gertrude Street
items.description: Melbourne's original bohemian quarter and still its most characterful, independent boutiques, record shops, wine bars and some of the city's best small dining. The neighbourhood to walk slowly with a coffee and let the family drift.

items.name: Collingwood & Smith Street
items.description: Once industrial, now the city's hottest strip, Smith Street runs from cult roasters to natural-wine bars and the rooftop of the old Foy & Gibson warehouses. A cool-hunter's afternoon for younger travellers.

items.name: Brunswick, Sydney Road & Lygon Street north
items.description: A multicultural strip of Middle Eastern grocers, live-music rooms and third-wave cafes, north of the centre and refreshingly un-touristed. Good for a driver to loop through for a taste of the real, everyday Melbourne.

items.name: Lygon Street, Carlton, Little Italy
items.description: The historic Italian quarter where Melbourne's espresso culture began, lined with trattorias and gelaterie. An easy, crowd-pleasing dinner street a short hop from the Exhibition Building and museum.

items.name: St Kilda Pier & the little-penguin colony
items.description: A newly rebuilt pier reaching into Port Phillip Bay, where around 1,400 wild little penguins come ashore at dusk on the breakwater, free to view from the boardwalk. A magical, gentle evening for children; go at sunset and keep torches off.

items.name: Luna Park Melbourne
items.description: The 1912 amusement park behind its famous grinning Mr Moon face on the Esplanade, home to one of the world's oldest continually operating roller-coasters (the Scenic Railway). Nostalgic and photogenic; open weekends and holidays.

items.name: The Esplanade & St Kilda foreshore
items.description: Melbourne's bayside promenade, palm-lined beach, Sunday art market, and the grand old Espy hotel, an easy seaside afternoon 15 minutes from the CBD. Cakes on Acland Street's continental-cake row are a ritual.

items.name: Southbank & the Yarra promenade
items.description: The riverside arts-and-dining precinct across from Flinders Street, Arts Centre spire, restaurants along the water, and the launch point for river cruises. A pleasant sundown stroll with the skyline reflected in the Yarra.

items.name: Yarra River cruise
items.description: A relaxed way to read the city from the water, sightseeing cruises run upriver toward the gardens and downriver to Docklands and the port. Charter a private vessel for a multi-gen group; a slow, low-effort highlight for elders.

items.name: Docklands & The District
items.description: A modern waterfront quarter of marinas, waterside dining and public art west of the CBD, reached by the free City Circle tram. Calmer than the centre and good for a harbourside lunch; the Melbourne Star wheel here is undergoing a planned reopening.

items.name: Arts Centre Melbourne
items.description: Under its lattice spire, the city's flagship performing-arts complex, ballet, opera, theatre and the Melbourne Symphony at Hamer Hall. Worth a night out; the Sunday market of makers runs along its forecourt.

items.name: Abbotsford Convent
items.description: A 19th-century convent turned rambling arts precinct on the riverbank, galleries, artist studios, gardens and the excellent Lentil As Anything and Convent Bakery. Free to wander, deeply atmospheric, and next to Collingwood Children's Farm for the little ones.

items.name: Fitzroy Gardens & Cooks' Cottage
items.description: A grand formal park on the CBD's edge, with elm avenues, a fairy tree and the transplanted stone cottage of Captain Cook's family, shipped brick-by-brick from England. A short, shaded green stop for elders between sights.

items.name: Chinatown & Little Bourke Street
items.description: One of the oldest continuous Chinatowns in the Western world, its arches spanning Little Bourke Street, with the Chinese Museum tucked among the restaurants. The address for late dumplings and the setting of Flower Drum.

items.name: Flower Drum
items.description: Melbourne's legendary Cantonese fine-diner, quietly running for over forty years on Market Lane, Peking duck, aromatic baked crab, and discreet, faultless service. The special-occasion dinner for a discerning family; book well ahead.

items.name: Chin Chin
items.description: The buzzing, all-day Southeast Asian diner on Flinders Lane that has drawn queues since 2011, hawker-style shared plates built for a table of many. Lively, generous and easy for a mixed group; the 'Feed Me' menu takes the decisions away.

items.name: Vue de Monde
items.description: Melbourne's landmark fine-dining room on the 55th floor of the Rialto, a native-ingredient degustation with the whole city at your feet. The city's dress-up dinner; request a window and let the sommelier lead.

items.name: Attica
items.description: Ben Shewry's celebrated suburban restaurant, long ranked among the world's best, serving a deeply personal tasting menu of native Australian ingredients. A pilgrimage table for serious food travellers; reservations open in advance and go fast.

items.name: Flinders Lane dining
items.description: The single best street to eat in Melbourne, a dense run of hatted restaurants and wine bars from Movida's tapas to Cumulus Inc. Let a concierge match the room to your group; walkable end to end.

items.name: Melbourne coffee crawl
items.description: Coffee is a genuine civic craft here, a private roaster-hopping morning through hole-in-the-wall bars and single-origin cafes reveals the culture better than any sight. Ask for a barista-led tasting; the flat white is the local benchmark.

items.name: Yarra Valley wineries (day trip)
items.description: An hour east, Victoria's premier cool-climate wine region, cellar doors from Domaine Chandon's French sparkling house to acclaimed Pinot and Chardonnay estates, with long lunches among the vines. Ideal as a chauffeured day; several estates cater beautifully to non-drinkers and families.

items.name: Great Ocean Road & the Twelve Apostles (day trip)
items.description: One of the world's great coastal drives, curling past surf beaches and rainforest to the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles rising from the Southern Ocean. A long but unforgettable full day; a private car and a helicopter add-on over the Apostles turn it into a highlight of the whole trip.

items.name: Mornington Peninsula & Peninsula Hot Springs (day trip)
items.description: Ninety minutes south, a coast of vineyards, beach boxes and Australia's largest natural hot-springs bathing complex, geothermal pools and a hilltop bath with bay views. A restorative day for elders and couples; pair the springs with a peninsula winery lunch.

items.name: Phillip Island Penguin Parade (day trip)
items.description: Around two hours south-east, the nightly spectacle of hundreds of little penguins waddling ashore after dusk, watched from boardwalks and tiered stands. Book premium or underground-viewing tickets for the family; the island also offers koalas and the Nobbies coast.

items.name: Dandenong Ranges & Puffing Billy (day trip)
items.description: An hour east into fern-gullied mountain forest, riding the century-old Puffing Billy steam train with legs dangling from open carriages, pure delight for children and grandparents alike. Add the William Ricketts sanctuary and a Sassafras tea room.

items.name: Sovereign Hill, Ballarat (day trip)
items.description: A vast, living re-creation of a 1850s gold-rush town about 90 minutes west, costumed streets, gold panning, and a nightly sound-and-light show. Immersive and hands-on for multi-generation groups curious about how Victoria's wealth was made.

items.name: Werribee Park Mansion & Shadowfax (day trip)
items.description: A grand 1870s Italianate mansion in formal gardens 30 minutes south-west, beside Shadowfax winery and the Werribee Open Range Zoo. A gentle, elegant half-day that combines heritage, wine and a safari-style drive for children.

items.name: Melbourne's parks & gardens promenade
items.description: The linked chain of parkland ringing the CBD, Kings Domain, Alexandra Gardens and the riverbank, makes for a long, level walk or a hired-bike loop past the Shrine and the rowing sheds. An easy way to see the city's famed green ring.

items.name: Australian Open (seasonal, January)
items.description: The year's first tennis Grand Slam, drawing the world to Melbourne Park each January, night sessions under lights at Rod Laver Arena are electric. Corporate suites and premium hospitality make it a marquee outing; book the season far ahead.

items.name: Australian Grand Prix (seasonal, March)
items.description: Formula 1 returns to the parkland circuit around Albert Park Lake each autumn, a fast street-style track minutes from the CBD. Trackside paddock and grandstand packages suit a group of enthusiasts; the city hums all weekend.

items.name: Melbourne Cup Carnival (seasonal, November)
items.description: 'The race that stops a nation', the first Tuesday of November at Flemington, the centrepiece of a spring carnival of fashion, marquees and champagne. The Birdcage enclosure is the ticket for a memorable, dressed-up day.

plan.heading: 3 days in Melbourne, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into the Hotel Windsor or Como, then the laneways and the NGV International's collection.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Coffee in the arcades and Hardware Lane, and the Royal Botanic Gardens along the Yarra.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Attica in Ripponlea, Ben Shewry's native-ingredient tasting menu, a 50 Best regular.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to the Yarra Valley or Mornington Peninsula for the cool-climate estates.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A cellar-door lunch, Ten Minutes by Tractor or the Oakridge dining room.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back in town, dinner at Cutler & Co. in Fitzroy.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Queen Victoria Market and the design shops of Gertrude Street, Fitzroy.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Ian Potter Centre at Federation Square for Australian art.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Flower Drum, the city's long-standing Cantonese institution in Chinatown.

items.name: Southbank / CBD
items.description: Central, by the river and the arts precinct; the convenient base for a first visit.

items.name: Fitzroy
items.description: Inner-north and creative, thick with bars and record shops; suits those chasing the local scene.

items.name: St Kilda
items.description: Bayside, relaxed and a little faded-glamorous; for travellers who want the beach and the promenade.

events.name: Australian Open
events.note: The year's first tennis Grand Slam, taking over Melbourne Park for a fortnight.

events.name: Melbourne International Comedy Festival
events.note: The world's largest dedicated comedy festival, hundreds of shows across the city.

events.name: Melbourne Cup Carnival
events.note: The race that stops a nation, the centrepiece of the spring racing weeks.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Melbourne rewards the curious: its best bars, cafes and restaurants hide down unmarked laneways, so a good local guide is worth it; day-trip to the Yarra Valley wineries or the Great Ocean Road, and pack layers as the weather turns in an afternoon.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Tullamarine (MEL), a 30 to 40-minute chauffeured drive into the centre; a private car is the right call as there is no rail link from the airport.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The compact grid is made for walking, and the free City Circle trams cover the centre; keep a private driver for the wineries and the coast.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Telstra or Optus) delivers strong 5G citywide; wifi is everywhere.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Australian dollar; cards and contactless are universal and cash is seldom needed; tipping is modest, around 10 percent when you wish.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Famous for 'four seasons in a day'; Mar-Apr (autumn) and Oct-Nov (spring) are the most settled, Dec-Feb is warm but can spike to sudden heat, and Jun-Aug is cold, grey and wet.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India in the standard schedule; route via Singapore (Singapore Airlines) or via Delhi/Sydney on Air India. Qantas runs a seasonal Delhi-Melbourne service 26 Oct 2026 to late Mar 2027. Fly Singapore Airlines business via Changi for the cleanest connection; pack layers, Melbourne weather turns fast.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; the same strict biosecurity applies, declare all food on arrival. Tap water is safe and healthcare is world-class. Melbourne is very safe. Weather swings are the main practical planning point.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Outstanding for vegetarians and Jain diets; a deep Indian community, superb pure-veg and South Indian restaurants, and a cafe culture that treats vegetarian and vegan as standard. Indian food along Sydney Road and in the eastern suburbs is genuinely good.
